body.head: At Walt Whitman’s Deathbed: The 1891-92 Leaves of Grass

div.p: Like many of Walt Whitman’s readers, my introduction to Leaves of Grass was the “Deathbed Edition.” Though my high school literature anthology contained only two of his poems, I sensed in Whitman something kindred and purchased the least expensive edition I could find: the Signet Classics paperback that promised me “the content and grouping of poems authorized by the poet for the final and complete edition of his masterpiece.” Walking home from the bookshop, I started reading, logically, the first poem of the first grouping and pressed forward. And like many of Whitman’s readers, I quickly found the nearly four hundred poems of Leaves of Grass to be a complicated puzzle without much of a guide. Not having studied Whitman’s life, I keenly sensed my lack of context for each grouping—at some point I learned that Whitman called them “clusters”—though I was still able to sit in awe with individual poems and sequences that struck me. I’ll never forget that Signet Classics Leaves of Grass; it was the first book I ever owned that, thrillingly, disintegrated from overuse. I agreed with its blurb that Leaves of Grass was a “masterpiece,” and supplying the necessary context to understand it became a decades-long study of Whitman’s life and nineteenth-century America.

I do not think my experience of the Deathbed Edition was unusual. Readers often find it disorienting, even with the guidance of introductions by scholars, historians, or poets that many publishers provide. Those readers who persist with Whitman usually seek out his writing in more straightforward and focused packaging. The twelve-poem first edition of Leaves of Grass from 1855 enjoys a wide popularity and has even been read as an American scripture. Readers discerning in Whitman what I first sensed in my high school textbook revel in standalone printings of “Calamus” and “Live Oak, with Moss.” Those who admire the Civil War docupoetics of “Drum-Taps” and “Memories of President Lincoln” now often encounter them in reissues of the self-contained Drum-Taps and Sequel to Drum-Taps, rather than as clusters in Leaves of Grass. These are in addition to the numerous compilations of selected poems and excerpts available.

Biographer and historian Gary Schmidgall acknowledges this retreat from the tangled and unwieldy Deathbed Edition of Leaves of Grass and toward Whitman’s earlier and more manageable work. In his introduction to Walt Whitman: Selected Poems 1855-1892, Schmidgall speaks for generations of “distinguished readers” who “agree that this long period of revision and accretion amounted to a devolution rather than an evolution.” While Whitman published over one hundred new poems from 1881 to 1892, Schmidgall’s volume includes only thirty-three from this period, selecting those that break from the aging Whitman’s “chaotic, unedifying, and, truth to tell, occasionally tedious form” that, in Schmidgall’s estimation, tends toward the “unremarkable or bombastic.” In making this stylistic claim, too, Schmidgall captures the estimation of many readers who encounter Whitman’s Deathbed Edition and other late life work.

It is evident, however, that the late Whitman felt differently about his final edition of Leaves of Grass. On the evening of January 23, 1892, Horace Traubel brought copies from Whitman’s publisher, David McKay, bound in dark green cloth. Traubel records the poet turning the book over in his hands by candlelight, saying, “this, of course, is the edition I swear by,” and offering revisions for the wording stamped on the spine, insisting on “Complete 1892.” It should be unmistakable to readers, “not casually, but radically,” Whitman argued, that although “we have had editions and editions and editions, this is to be in “future the only authentic and perfect.” He liked even the book’s unwieldiness because he felt in its heft the weight of his life’s work: “What a book it makes now—how plump! And with a pretty touch, too, as made up in this shape.” Decades of growth brought Leaves of Grass into a buxom fullness far from its slim and lithe 1855 debut (see Table 1 for the contents of the 1855 Leaves of Grass and its relationship to the contents of the Deathbed Edition).

Though Whitman insisted that the spine be labeled “1892,” its title page bears the expanded date of “1891-’2” beneath the publisher’s information. Ever since the third edition of Leaves of Grass, with its hyphenated “1860-61” on the title page, Whitman liked hyphenated dates. Encountering these, one might assume that the first year is the work’s date of copyright and the second of its distribution, but there are other books with differing dates on the copyright and title pages that Whitman (and Whitman scholars) did not span, such as Passage to India and Two Rivulets. So when Whitman’s title pages include a span—as do Memoranda During the War and Specimen Days & Collect, and the 1881-82 edition of Leaves of Grass—it suggests a certain authorial calculation. Ed Folsom, for example, notes that the third edition’s dating ominously portends “the final year of unstable peace with the first year of actual war,” an augury that is reversed with the “1865-6” Sequel to Drum-Taps, “straddling the last year of war and the first year of reconstruction.” Although the fifth edition of Leaves of Grass was copyrighted and sold in 1870, it is dated 1871 and was expanded in 1872, and has been known colloquially as the “1871-72 edition” (and is so identified in the Whitman Encyclopedia). Ten years later, Whitman placed the spanned date of 1881-82 on the title page of the edition published by James Osgood, and 1891-’92 on the one from David McKay ten years after that. These three editions mark successive ten-year intervals, with the final span portending Whitman’s last full year of corporeality and the year his afterlife commenced.

Each edition is an episode in the growth of Leaves of Grass, yet Whitman wrote in a letter to Richard Maurice Bucke that “to me the 1892 ed’n supersedes them all by far” (duk.00962; despite the span on the title page, Whitman nearly always referred to this as the “‘92 Edition” in conversation and correspondence). And as letters arrived from friends and admirers who received this latest printing, Traubel dutifully read to Whitman from those who celebrated it as a crowning achievement. Later, when discussing a volume of Selected Poems published by Charles Webster, Whitman told Traubel, “I know of nothing more essential to our purposes than to have the world realize the approved volume—the ‘92 edition—as the only really complete and satisfactory presentation of our case.” While Whitman did not affix the adjective “deathbed” to this printing—as this introduction will consider after an outline of the 1892 edition’s contents—the adjectives he uses in conversation and correspondence are bold: complete, authentic, perfect, approved.

From its opening pages, the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass insists on its completeness, tucking “Copyrights &c.” behind the title page. Following a bibliographic list of every edition from 1855 onward and its annexes (the “copyrights”), Whitman included an initialled notice (the “&c.”) that commands his readers’ attention with the printer’s manicule:
☞As there are now several editions of L. of G., different texts and dates, I wish to say that I prefer and recommend this present one, complete, for future printing, if there should be any; a copy and fac-simile, indeed, of the text of these 438 pages. The subsequent adjusting interval which is so important to form’d and launch’d work, books especially, has pass’d; and waiting till fully after that, I have given (pages 423-438) my concluding words.
Reprints of the Deathbed Edition are inconsistent in their inclusion of “Copyrights &c.,” as they are also with their inclusion of the closing “Backward Glance” essay. The list of copyrights for Leaves of Grass calls attention to those “editions and editions and editions” that Whitman mentioned to Traubel. But even as he softens his authorial directive into a preference and recommendation, Whitman is clear that the “adjusting interval” from 1855 to 1892, during which he tinkered with the structure of Leaves of Grass, is over. He is like a prophet declaring the end of the dispensation; with this edition, the canon has closed and there will be no new revelation.

That “adjusting interval” lasted well over three decades, longer if the pre-1855 manuscripts that led to its inception are considered. Each edition—and there are anywhere from six to ten, depending on how a given commentator classifies an “edition”—is a milestone toward the book’s final destination, which Whitman identifies as the ninth edition. (Throughout, I prefer to follow Whitman’s lead in referring to the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass as an “edition.”) As becomes evident when comparing each printing from Whitman’s lifetime, these milestones can be radically different from one to another. At some point, the process had to reach an end.

When Whitman told Traubel that the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass was “the only authentic and perfect” one, he likely did not intend perfect to mean “flawless,” but rather in its use as a synonym for “complete,” the word that he directed to be stamped on its spine. He was aware that shaping the book into its final form left noticeable seams. When he sent a paperbound copy to Bucke on December 6, 1891, Whitman reminisced on the “33 yr’s of hackling at it all times & moods of my life, fair weather & foul, all parts of the land, and peace & war, young & old” (loc.08213). He acknowledges that its present form has “numerous deficiencies & faults” and is characterized by a certain “jaggedness.” Yet, Whitman writes, the “cumulus character of the book is a great factor.” Cumulus, from the Latin, an uneven heap, a growing mass.

Responding to a letter of effusive praise in receipt of the paperbound book from his close friend Robert G. Ingersoll, Whitman confessed that he was aware of “its numberless deficiencies,” but that he was especially proud of two aspects of this “complete” Leaves of Grass: “the atmosphere & the notion of all, whatever it is being in process (evolution) from first page to last” (prc.00140). Frustrated readers of the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass may have trouble accepting the book’s jaggedness and deficiencies, but Whitman suggested these were indicators of its decades-long organic growth. These readers can thus learn to forgive, and perhaps even to embrace, the book’s messiness, just as the Japanese principle of wabi-sabi invites us to find beauty in asymmetry and imperfections.

div.head: The Deathbed Edition’s Messy Structure
div.p: Any introduction to the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass will need to include an outline of the book’s structure, walking through its divisions and the ways Whitman organized his poems, while keeping in mind this principle of wabi-sabi. As Whitman asserts in a “Calamus” poem, “these leaves and me you will not understand . . . even while you should think you had unquestionably caught me, behold! Already you see I have escaped from you.” That the “Copyrights &c.” notice faces the book’s table of contents should remind readers of the composite and, as Whitman would have it, the jagged nature of Leaves of Grass. Each of the previous editions and supplements identified in Whitman’s list contributed to the final form, coalescing unevenly around the 1855 edition like the crystalline accretions of a geode.

While modifications to the structure of Leaves of Grass during the “adjusting interval” were often quite dramatic, the arrangement of the Deathbed Edition follows its last major redesign in 1881, the plates of which Whitman used as its basis, together with a handful of minor punctuation changes he made for an 1888 impression, and the two annexes, “Sands at Seventy” and “Good-Bye My Fancy,” containing his poems published since the 1881 edition. Also new to the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass is the concluding essay, “A Backward Glance O’er Travel’d Roads.” Since each entry in the Table of Contents to Leaves of Grass could receive its own lengthy exposition, this introduction’s whirlwind tour must consist mainly of the highlights and, frankly, a few lowlights. For more thorough information on major poems and clusters, see Walt Whitman: An Encyclopedia, edited by J. R. LeMaster and Donald D. Kummings (available on the Walt Whitman Archive).

Whitman offers his readers poetry even before the list of copyrights and the table of contents, however. The title page of the Deathbed Edition includes the nine-line epigraphic poem which begins, “Come, said my soul,” that Whitman first included in the same place in the 1876 “Author’s Edition,” a repackaging of the fifth edition of 1871. Whitman personally autographed nearly every copy of that Author’s Edition, literalizing the poem’s concluding enactment, “I here and now, signing for Soul and Body, set to them my name, [Walt Whitman].” The poem is absent from the 1881 Leaves of Grass but reappeared in 1888’s Complete Poems & Prose on the title page for its inclusion of Leaves of Grass—where again Whitman signed every copy. In 1892, Whitman’s signature was printed in facsimile rather than autographed, “set” now on the page by his printers, but his intention still stands that “should I after death invisibly return . . . I may keep on, ever and ever yet the verses owning.” Whitman included the poem as a convenient place for his autograph in 1876 and 1888, and also as a confirmation that he personally handled every copy. In 1892, the poem and its printed autograph mimic that authorial closeness, hinting at the book as a bridge between life and death, past and future, author and reader. This recurring and mystical secret, introduced on the very first leaf of Leaves of Grass, becomes a driving theme in poems like “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry,” and those found in the “Songs of Parting” cluster.

Mimicking authorial closeness was one of Whitman’s special skills. Starting in 1871, Leaves of Grass opens with the twenty-four poem “Inscriptions” cluster, which grew from a single introductory poem titled “Inscription” in the fourth edition (1867). These inscription poems tend to be quite short, most ranging from two to eight lines, with the longest being the 1876 poem, “Eidólons,” composed of twenty-one quatrains. Though they were never literally inscribed into the book by the poet himself, the poems directly address the owner of the book and its current readers like an author’s handwritten inscription on a book’s flyleaf—and there are many examples of these from Whitman, too. The dedications hail a multifarious audience, including “To Foreign Lands,” “To a Historian,” “To the States,” “To a Certain Cantatrice,” and “To You.” Whitman imagines the “proud libraries” for whom Leaves of Grass supplies “that which was lacking on all your well-fill’d shelves” (“Shut Not Your Doors”). For those surrounded by hostile forces, Leaves of Grass will be “a commander, swift, brave, immortal” and with a full artillery, “the deadliest that ever fired gun” (“What Place Is Besieged”). To wordsmiths of future generations, Leaves of Grass presents but “one or two indicative words” while “expecting the main things from you” (“Poets to Come”).

After the inscription poems, Leaves of Grass truly commences with “Starting from Paumanok,” a poem with nineteen sections and nearly three hundred lines that first appeared as the “Proto-Leaf” to the 1860 edition. In nearly every edition since—with the exception of 1871, where it is followed by three short poems later moved elsewhere—it has immediately preceded the long poem that came to be called “Song of Myself.” As in the “Inscriptions” cluster, Whitman emphasizes the relationship between himself and his reader, his “camerado close,” offering the rough sketch of an autobiography that notes his childhood on Long Island (“Paumanok” in Algonquin) and career in Manhattan as a “lover of populous pavements,” before spiraling outward into other generic American identities far beyond the historical Walt Whitman, including a California gold miner and “a soldier camp’d or carrying my knapsack and gun.” This self composed of many selves hints at the “multitudes” that Whitman famously claims to contain in “Song of Myself.” By design, all the major themes of Leaves of Grass, and many of its significant images, appear in “Starting from Paumanock.” It is the closest Whitman comes to providing a “road map” to Leaves of Grass.

Whitman’s road map poem, which scholar Ivan Marki likens to “an overture to one of the poet’s beloved Italian operas,” communicates the intentions of Leaves of Grass in simple future tense, whose repetitions have an incantatory quality. “I will” appears twenty-nine times, often foreshadowing some poem or cluster that the reader encounters later in the volume: “I will report all heroism from an American point of view . . . I will write the evangel-poem of comrades and of love . . . I will be the bard of personality . . . I will show that nothing can happen more beautiful than death.” But while these intentions may suggest a sundry list, “Starting from Paumanok” explains that all the poems to come will share some combination of three “greatnesses,” capitalized by Whitman in section 10: Love, Democracy, and Religion. It is as if these three themes are the components of a Venn Diagram into which each poem of Leaves of Grass can be placed, whether in their union, intersection, or complement.

After “Starting from Paumanok,” Whitman launches into his central poetic thesis, “Song of Myself.” If the former poem is the overture introducing the leitmotifs of Leaves of Grass, then the latter poem is its first act aria. Some form of “Song of Myself” has been in every edition since 1855, where it opened the book’s twelve-poem cycle with its famous line, “I celebrate myself.” This line was the working title that Whitman gave the poem when sketching out the table of contents for the printers prior to the 1855 publication; and although every other poem debuted in a different order than his initial sketch, “I Celebrate Myself” was to be the opener (tex.00001; the manuscript does not indicate that the book would include the prose preface). Yawping for over thirteen-hundred lines, “Song of Myself” is Whitman’s longest poem. And while the poet edited it for the subsequent editions of Leaves of Grass—including playing with different titles, adding and removing lines, and eventually dividing the whole thing into fifty-two numbered sections—it always retained its pride of place.

Appropriate to a poem of such central importance, much ink has been spilled over “Song of Myself.” It continues to be a core text to our understanding of Whitman because, like “Starting from Paumanok,” it contains all those key “Whitmanic” themes he identified as shades of Love, Democracy, and Religion. In the new millennium, the freshly edited Oxford Book of American Poetry included “Song of Myself” in its entirety; the poem was fully “illuminated” by artist Allen Crawford for Tin House Books; and it received a thorough section-by-section commentary by Ed Folsom and Christopher Merrill of the University of Iowa. Documentary filmmaker Jennifer Crandall initiated the “Whitman, Alabama” project in 2017 to record residents of the state reading “Song of Myself” as “an experiment in using documentary and poetry to reveal the threads that tie us together—as people, as states, and as a nation.” In whatever format readers continue to encounter the poem, many still take up Whitman’s summons to “loafe with me on the grass,” a botanical symbol later revealed to be “no less than the journey-work of the stars” and even the embodiment of his own continued existence, leading to his further invitation for readers to “look for me under your boot-soles.”

“Song of Myself” is flanked by poetic accretions from the 1860 Leaves of Grass, with “Starting from Paumanok” preceding it and the “Children of Adam” and “Calamus” clusters following. Manuscripts leading to these latter groupings suggest that Whitman envisioned them as a complementary pair, one dedicated to a male speaker’s encounter of “the passion of Woman-Love” and the other “to adhesiveness, manly love” between men (duk.00279; see also uva.00086). In them, Whitman expands his central poem’s celebration of the self: the often sexually-explicit poems in “Children of Adam” aim to “celebrate you act divine and you children prepared for, and you stalwart loins” (“From Pent-Up Aching Rivers”) while Whitman’s urge “to tell the secret of my nights and days, / To celebrate the need of comrades” determines the homoerotic tenderness of “Calamus” (“In Paths Untrodden”).

If Whitman intended the clusters to be complementary expressions of heteroerotic and homoerotic intimacy, however, he never succeeded at their equilibrium. In the 1860 Leaves of Grass, the Francofied “Enfans d’Adam” premiered at fifteen numbered poems and “Calamus” at forty-five. As is frequently the case with Whitman’s clusters, they were adjusted from edition to edition and contain poems from various iterations of Leaves of Grass, with “Children of Adam” even including one, “I Sing the Body Electric,” that first appeared in the original 1855 series of twelve poems. It is indicative of Whitman’s personal erotic orientation that at thirty-nine poems, the Deathbed Edition’s “Calamus” continues to far outweigh “Children of Adam” at just sixteen. Indeed, it seems as if Whitman was hard pressed to glean heterosexual love poems from his voluminous manuscripts, and in at least one known instance, changed the sex of a male lover to address the shortage of “Children of Adam” poems (uva.00183).

After steeping in these two “love” clusters, readers might assume that Leaves of Grass will proceed in thematic groupings. Such a tidy organization would not be wabi-sabi, however. The next dozen poems, which mostly debuted in the first three editions and cover nearly seventy pages, are unassigned and without a unifying theme. Whitman identifies eight of them as “songs,” as if these twelve disparate poems present his own Great American Songbook—and composers have set several of them to music, such as Matthew Greenbaum’s 2019 “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry,” a “monodrama for baritone and strings.” From the 1856 Leaves of Grass came the three poems that open Whitman’s songbook—“Salut Au Monde!,” “Song of the Open Road,” and “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry”—as well as “Song of the Broad-Axe” and “A Song of the Rolling Earth.” These 1856 poems are perhaps the most read, commented on, and beloved selections from this portion of Leaves of Grass.

Three lesser-read poems that preserve lines from the 1855 edition demonstrate Whitman’s tinkering with the arrangement of Leaves of Grass: “A Song for Occupations” immediately followed “Song of Myself” in the 1855 cycle, “Youth, Day, Old Age and Night” is a fragment of the cycle’s twelfth and concluding poem (which concludes this “songbook” portion of the Deathbed Edition), and “Song of the Answerer” pieces together the seventh poem from 1855 and lines from the prose preface. “Our Old Feuillage” and “A Song of Joys” from 1860 are back-to-back, though they are less celebrated than the poems from the 1860 clusters earlier in Leaves of Grass.

The only poems in the songbook that do not derive from the three pre-war editions, “Song of the Exposition” and “Song of the Redwood Tree,” nod to Whitman’s experimental Two Rivulets from 1876, where they appear in the same order they are found in Leaves of Grass. The first was written in 1871 as a public recitation for the American Institute in New York, and first published as a pamphlet under the title of its first line, After All, Not to Create Only. “Song of the Redwood Tree” first appeared in an 1874 issue of Harper's New Monthly Magazine. When compiling Two Rivulets, Whitman placed the poems prominently together at the beginning of “Centennial Songs,” though neither are considered masterful examples of his style—and have even been derided as poems indicating his stylistic decline, with Schmidgall’s Selected Poems excluding both.

Following the twelve poem songbook, Leaves of Grass returns to clusters with “Birds of Passage,” which gathers poems from 1856 to 1876. Despite this return to groupings, however, the principle of wabi-sabi is still in play, as the assemblage has puzzled readers and scholars since it first appeared in the 1881 edition. As might be expected of poems written over a twenty year span, the voice, themes, and images vary a great deal, reflecting in miniature the accretionary structure of the final edition of Leaves of Grass, in which late-life “annexes” recontextualize the mid-life poetic voice still couched within the larger frame. I suggest that this cluster’s title is a self-consciously poetic gesture, since Whitman borrowed it from the most celebrated—and lucrative—American poet of his generation, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. Longfellow used the title for the grouping of twenty-three “other poems” in his 1858 book, The Courtship of Miles Standish and Other Poems. In this bestseller that famously sold 10,000 copies in London in a single day and 25,000 domestically in its first two months, “Birds of Passage” opens with an Italian epigraph from Canto 5 of Dante’s Inferno: “. . . come i gru van cantando lor lai, / faccendo in aere di sé lunga riga” (“as the cranes go chanting forth their lays, / Making in air a long line of themselves,” in Longfellow’s later translation of Inferno). Like the cluster in Leaves of Grass, Longfellow’s “Birds of Passage” has no recurring image or theme, it is merely a compilation—“a long line” of poems. The unifying theme of Whitman’s “Birds of Passage,” then, is perhaps not to be found in the poems themselves, but in Whitman’s striving to be taken seriously as a poet and for Leaves of Grass to be ranked among the masterpieces of literature.

Commentaries arguing for “Birds of Passage” as a transition from the younger to the more mature poetic voice within Leaves of Grass are undermined by the poem Whitman placed immediately following the cluster: “A Broadway Pageant.” This poem first appeared in an 1860 issue of the New York Times and was included in the 1865 Drum-Taps, where it bears the useful subscript, “Reception Japanese Embassy, June 16, 1860,” placing it in history as a celebration of the first treaty between the United States and Japan. Since it predates the eruption of the American Civil War, it makes sense that it does not appear in the “Drum-Taps” cluster of Leaves of Grass, though it is uncertain why Whitman did not assign it to any other cluster.

Again, Leaves of Grass returns to clusters with “Sea-Drift” and “By the Roadside,” both of which first appeared in the 1881 edition (either one could have been a good fit for “A Broadway Pageant,” but, once again, wabi-sabi). Whitman first clustered the “Sea-Drift” poems together as “Sea-Shore Memories” for the 1871 Passage to India, a sort of “Whitman sampler” that paired new poems with previously-published material from periodicals and Leaves of Grass. The current cluster opens with two poems from the 1860 edition, “Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking” and “As I Ebb’d with the Ocean of Life,” returning readers to the shores of Paumanok and musing on central themes from Leaves of Grass. While dying has featured prominently in poems like “Song of Myself” where the book’s titular grass is revealed to be “the beautiful uncut hair of graves,” it is reiterated and stressed in “Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking,” where the ocean “lisp’d to me the low and delicious word death / And again death, death, death, death, . . . / Death, death, death, death, death.” Readers must confront this troubling word until it no longer frightens them—important preparation for the “Drum-Taps” cluster soon to come as well as the “Whispers of Heavenly Death” and “Songs of Parting” groupings that close the 1881 Leaves of Grass. The 1891 annexes fully conjoin living and dying, which are revealed to be “two old, simple problems ever intertwined,” and “two mighty masterful vessels” that “steal upon us.”

As the “Sea-Drift” cluster’s second poem emphasizes, the “ocean of life” ebbs; life and death are in a constant push-and-pull relationship like successive waves on the shore. These two early poems foreground the marine “life and death” metaphor that prevents a flattening of the nautical images in the cluster’s nine short lyrical poems that date from later editions. In the 1891 “Good-Bye My Fancy” annex, a note to the poem “An Ended Day” literalizes this symbol of life’s ebbing tide while meditating on Whitman’s volunteer work during the Civil War: “visiting the Army Hospitals around Washington, I form’d the habit, and continued it to the end, whenever the ebb or flood tide began the latter part of day, of punctually visiting those at that time populous wards of suffering men.” The Civil War’s massive toll on human life ensured that the poet was not alone in his ebbing with life’s ocean, when “the effect of the hour was palpable” and “Deaths were always easier.”

While the poems in “Sea-Drift” foreground marine images, “By the Roadside” has the feeling of a miscellany similar to “Birds of Passage.” Its unifying thread might be the observational aspect of many of its entries. “The Dalliance of the Eagles,” first published in the November 1880 issue of Cope’s Tobacco Plant, entered the 1881 Leaves of Grass as part of the new cluster and was central to the charges of obscenity brought by Boston District Attorney Oliver Stevens. As with previous clusters, “By the Roadside” gathers poems from various editions of Leaves of Grass, including two from 1855, “A Boston Ballad” and “Europe,” which appeared ninth and eighth in the original twelve-poem cycle, respectively. Five poems, including notably “When I heard the Learn’d Astronomer,” first appeared in the 1865 Drum-Taps and were moved elsewhere when poems from that volume were incorporated into Leaves of Grass to sharpen “Drum-Taps”’s thematic focus on experiences of the Civil War. As is easily observed, Whitman’s poems tend to get shorter later in his career, and the two 1855 poems are the longest entries in “By the Roadside”—they are among the shortest poems in the first edition—while twelve of the cluster’s twenty-nine poems have fewer than three lines. Short poems like “Mother and Babe” and “A Farm Picture” often strike readers with a masterful imagistic quality, however, which they retain even when presented in rapid sequence.

“By the Roadside” concludes with the pre-war political poem “To the States, To Identify the 16th, 17th, or 18th Presidentiad,” first printed in the 1860 Leaves of Grass. Whitman had eagerly hoped his “New Bible” would dispel the “gathering murk” of civil conflict that loomed over his nation, and this poem sharply criticises the administrations of Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce, and James Buchanan, that directly contributed to the violent rift between northern and southern states. Whitman’s hopes that the union would be preserved were dashed in April 1861, with the eruption of the Civil War. Thus when reading the contents of the Deathbed Edition sequentially, “By the Roadside” transitions smoothly into the “Drum-Taps” and “Memories of President Lincoln” clusters.

The sesquicentennial of the Civil War from 2011 to 2015 brought increased focus on Whitman’s war experience, including the reissue of the 1865 Drum-Taps, edited and annotated by Lawrence Kramer for the New York Review of Books. This focus remains into the 2020s and enjoys a warm reception. Kenneth Price’s Whitman in Washington: Becoming the National Poet in the Federal City provides ample background to Whitman’s wartime service. In 2021, Folsom and Merrill released another commentary, “The Million Dead, Too, Summ’d Up”: Walt Whitman’s Civil War Writings, bringing together Whitman’s on-the-spot poetry and prose. Children’s author Gary Golio’s 2024 The Soldier’s Friend: Walt Whitman’s Extraordinary Service in the American Civil War, illustrated by E. B. Lewis has won several book awards.

As these popular works often stress, the Civil War marked a turning point in Whitman’s life, and “Drum-Taps” starts Leaves of Grass anew with “First O Songs for a Prelude,” which opened the standalone Drum-Taps volume published in 1865. Despite an opening that romanticises the “pride and joy in my city” at the beginning of the war and the New Yorkers Whitman saw “advancing to welcome it,” the cluster loses its jingoistic tone as it documents the suffering that Whitman witnessed first- and second-hand during his volunteer work in the army hospitals around Washington.

Mirroring the war-weariness of American soldiers and civilians, the longer the cluster continues, the darker its perspective becomes. Emotionally heavy poems like “Vigil Strange I Kept on the Field One Night” and “A Sight in Camp in the Daybreak Gray and Dim” offer little glamour. This heaviness remained with the poet for decades, as he portrays himself in the Deathbed Edition’s second annex as “musing on long-pass’d war-scenes—of the countless buried unknown soldiers,” and the war’s “grim burial-squads, and the deep-fill’d trenches of gather’d dead” (“Twilight Song”). Throughout the cluster, Whitman contrasts conventionally poetic, even flowery images with depictions of mass, weaponized death, epitomized in the four lines of “Look Down Fair Moon,” in which the poet implores the moon to “pour softly down night’s nimbus floods on faces ghastly, swollen, purple, / On the dead on their backs with arms toss’d wide,” strewn prolifically on an unidentified battlefield.

Reminiscing on “those agnostic and lurid” wartime years in “A Backward Glance O’er Travel’d Roads,” Whitman notes that “without those three or four years and the experiences they gave, Leaves of Grass would not now be existing.” That is to say, without witnessing America’s “gloom, despair, hopes again arous’d, courage evoked,” there would have been no post-war editions of Leaves of Grass. The book would have become an antebellum relic. Importantly, the “Drum-Taps” cluster tempers earlier themes in Leaves of Grass, including the optimism captured in the “Calamus” declaration that “I will make the continent indissoluble . . . by the manly love of comrades.” The “Camerado” of “Drum-Taps” confesses bleakly to his friend: “I have urged you onward with me, and still urge you, without the least idea what is our destination, / Or whether we shall be victorious, or utterly quell’d and defeated.” Given the scale of the American Civil War, personal comradeship and personal loss seemed small at times, especially following the assasination of president Abraham Lincoln that nationalized the grief over a fallen comrade. Whitman continued to temper the themes of Leaves of Grass with each augmentation, so that the Deathbed Edition encapsulates nearly three decades of Whitman’s evolving views of America, comradeship, and human suffering.

The “Memories of President Lincoln” cluster in Leaves of Grass offers four elegiac poems including the often-quoted “O Captain, My Captain.” In these poems, Lincoln is both a stand-in for and the culmination of each fallen American soldier, whose tally is still debated by historians and reaches anywhere from 500,000 to 750,000. While readers of poetry are rightly hesitant to attribute a poem’s “I” to the poet himself, Whitman speaks in “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d” not only as an eyewitness to the war’s slaughter, but he also speaks for many other Americans who shared his witness: “I saw battle-corpses, myriads of them, / And the white skeletons of young men, I saw them, / I saw the debris and debris of all the slain soldiers of the war.” These lines from section 15 turn on a realization of what all this carnage means for those who remain to pick up the pieces:
But I saw they were not as was thought,
They themselves were fully at rest, they suffer’d not,
The living remain’d and suffer’d, the mother suffer’d,
And the wife and the child and the musing comrade suffer’d,
And the armies that remain'd suffer’'d.
To survive is to suffer. And to survive today is to anticipate a death which comes on some inevitable tomorrow, a point Whitman experienced in his own body following the series of debilitating strokes that punctuated the last decades of his life and testified to in the poems in the Deathbed Edition’s annexes.

Readers can observe how the Civil War changed Leaves of Grass not only through the poems springing out of wartime experiences, but in the edits Whitman made to the poems from the antebellum editions. The next entry in the Table of Contents, “By Blue Ontario’s Shore,” is a prime example of Whitman editing the war into his poetry, with some lines originating in passages from the prose preface of the 1855 Leaves of Grass. Rarely appreciated as an artful specimen of Whitman’s craft, “By Blue Ontario’s Shore” alters the prewar themes of Love, Democracy, and Religion, bringing the poetic voice into the Reconconstruction era. “O I see flashing that this America is only you and me,” Whitman announces in lines originating from the poem's 1860 version. Lest he slip back into jingoism, Whitman adds in a line from 1867, “The war, (that war so bloody and grim, the war I will henceforth forget), was you and me,” reminding American readers of their own part in the massacres of the Civil War. While death has been a recurring motif in Leaves of Grass, the book grows preoccupied with it following the “Lincoln” cluster and pivots on this return to prewar themes forever tempered by musings “of these warlike days and of peace return’d, and the dead that return no more.”

It would abandon the principle of wabi-sabi, however, to follow these musings from “By Blue Ontario’s Shore” with the next cluster, “Autumn Rivulets.” Whitman interjects “Reversals” between them, though this six-line poem could have belonged to any of the more eclectic clusters. It originates from the much longer 1856 “Poem of The Propositions of Nakedness,” called “Respondez!” from 1860 until its renaming and truncation for the 1881 edition. In its longer form, the poem is filled with irony and fire, each line ending with an exclamation mark, often containing several within the line. These exclamation marks, colloquially called “screamers” by printers, and the contrasting ideals espoused in the poem give it the feel of a disparate collection of shouted slogans. Its current, shorter form is much softened, freed of those screamers, and with a deliberate echo of Jesus’ radical proposition that “the first shall be last, and the last first” (Matthew 20:16).

Like the preceding “Birds of Passage,” “Sea-Drift,” and “By The Roadside” clusters, “Autumn Rivulets” first appeared as a grouping in the 1881 Leaves of Grass and gathers poems spanning all previous editions, including two from 1855. While the cluster’s title suggests a thematic focus on the autumnal seasons of life, it preserves something of the vitality thrumming through the earlier poems in Leaves of Grass. The titular “rivulets” is perhaps intended to harken back to the unconventional Two Rivulets, whose juxtapositions of poetry and prose on the same page were meant to evoke the “streams of Death and Life.” Further suggesting this nod to the earlier volume, the cluster opens with the poem, “As Consequent, Etc.,” that grew out of the opening poems of Two Rivulets. In its current form, the poem likens the poet’s youthful output to “summer rains” that fed into the “wayward rivulets in autumn flowing,” and indicates that the cluster will contain the “songs of continued years.” This emphasis on continued years, rather than later years, might help readers wend through this miscellany of poems written over three decades and prepare them for the newly added late-life poems of the two annexes.

One notable inclusion, “To a Common Prostitute,” scandalized readers like Ralph Waldo Emerson and even the Boston publishers of the 1860 edition, Thayer and Eldridge, with its unapologetic sexuality. When a later publisher, James Osgood, proposed the poem’s removal from its current position in the 1881 edition in response to the charges of obscenity, Whitman took the plates to a new publisher, David McKay, and the poem remained. Although contained in the “Autumn Rivulets” cluster, the poem with its tender promise, “not till the sun excludes you do I exclude you,” might have been at home among the direct addresses of “Inscriptions.” It held a similar role among the 1860 edition’s “Messenger Leaves,” where it appeared with other missive poems now in “Autumn Rivulets”—“To a Foil’d European Revolutionaire,” “To Him That Was Crucified,” and “To a Pupil.”

Tucked between the “Autumn Rivulets” and “Whispers of Heavenly Death” clusters are six unassigned poems that have even less thematic consonance than the twelve “songbook” poems. The first two, “Proud Music of the Storm” and “Passage to India” featured prominently in the 1871 pamphlet, Passage to India. The third, “Prayer of Columbus,” first appeared in Harper’s Monthly and later in Two Rivulets. An assumption that perhaps these unclustered poems all share a post-war perspective is undermined by the inclusion of two poems from 1855, “The Sleepers” and “To Think of Time,” here separated by the three-line “Transpositions,” a sister poem to “Reversals” that also repurposes lines from the 1856 “Poem on The Propositions of Nakedness.” The symmetry of three poems written after the Civil War followed by three poems written before the war might be accidental rather than indicative of Whitman’s forethought. Then again, the intermingling of early and later poems in the second half of Leaves of Grass—both inside and outside the clusters—may be designed to force the reader into assuming thematic continuities in the contents of Leaves of Grass that are not explicitly given.

Leaves of Grass always celebrated life’s transitions, including death, but as Whitman faced his own mortality, the tenor of his poems dealing with the final transition grew ambivalent. Poems for “Whispers of Heavenly Death” were first put together in Passage to India, and additional poems added when the cluster was folded into the 1881 Leaves of Grass. Ten of the cluster’s eighteen poems appeared in pre-war editions, nearly balancing pre-war and post-war musings on death. Compiled after witnessing the wholesale slaughter of bodies and the breakdown of his own, the first of Whitman’s three concluding clusters opens with the uncertain, “Darest Thou Now O Soul.” The poet hesitates before the soul’s entry into “the unknown region” where “all is blank before us,” and while “all the ties loosen,” including the soul’s tethering to a material body, Time and Space remain in which to “float” disembodied. The cluster ends with the poet entirely dissolving his famous ego into “I the apparition, I the spectre” (“Pensive and Faltering”).

Even while pulling from the various editions of Leaves of Grass, the final three clusters, “Whispers of Heavenly Death,” “From Noon to Starry Night” and “Songs of Parting” demonstrate Whitman’s strength in crafting harmonic groupings. The flow from the first to the second of these, however, is interrupted by two unassigned poems: the oft-derided “Thou Mother with Thy Equal Brood,” written as a commencement address for Dartmouth’s 1872 graduating class and published in As a Strong Bird on Pinions Free; and the imagistic “A Paumanok Picture,” comprising seven lines excised from the 1856 poem later called “Salut Au Monde!” This latter poem with its ten fishermen in “two boats with nets lying off the sea-beach,” would have been at home in the “Sea-Drift” cluster, but here appears non-sequitur. The almost intrusive placement of these two poems before “From Noon to Starry Night” feels like the book’s hesitation to continue the meditations on mortality begun in “Whispers of Heavenly Death.”

“From Noon to Starry Night” is another career-spanning collection, reflected in the side-by-side placement of its two opening poems, “Thou Orb Aloft Full-Dazzling” from 1881 and the 1855 poem, “Faces.” Tracing its twenty-two poems to their first book appearances compiles a Whitman bibliography of its own. Not only are the first three editions of Leaves of Grass represented alongside poems new to the 1881 edition, but also Drum-Taps from 1865 (“Weave In, My Hardy Life” and “Thick-Sprinkled Bunting”), Sequel to Drum-Taps the following year (“Ah Poverties, Wincings, and Sulky Retreats” and “Old War Dreams”), As A Strong Bird on Pinions Free from 1872 (“The Mystic Trumpeter” and “By Broad Potomac’s Shore”), and Two Rivulets from 1876 (“To a Locomotive in Winter” and “Spain, 1873-74”). As with other groupings of poems in Leaves of Grass, some recurring motifs in “From Noon to Starry Night” can be inferred, including trajectories and juxtapositions, but the clearest unifying figure is Whitman’s poetic ego itself, which began its “noon” in 1855 with its all-seeing gaze like that of the meridian sun. At last, it approaches the “starry night” of the silence of death, expressed in “A Clear Midnight” as “the flight into the wordless / Away from books, away from art, the day erased, the lesson done.”

The 1881 arrangement of Leaves of Grass concludes with the seventeen-poem cycle, “Songs of Parting” introduced in the 1871 edition, though it opens and closes with poems from the 1860 edition. Testifying to the continued centrality of his wartime experience, the cluster also gathers poems from the 1865 Drum-Taps, including an invocation to the “ashes of soldiers South or North” that the final act of Leaves of Grass might include “perfume from battle-fields rising, up from the foetor arising.” Also in the cluster are two late-life elegies, one dedicated to his mother (“As at Thy Portals Also Death”) and the other to the assassinated president James Garfield (“The Sobbing of the Bells”). The six poems preceding the final “So Long!” preserve part of the longer “Now Finale to the Shore” sequence that closed the 1871 collection, Passage to India. The cluster ends with Whitman receding into “an unknown sphere more real than I dream’d,” offering his parting kisses to the reader as he becomes “one disembodied, triumphant, dead.” This powerful disincarnation closed every edition of Leaves of Grass between 1860 and 1881.

But disembodiment took Whitman longer than expected; he survived a full decade after the release of the 1881 Leaves of Grass, and continued to write and contribute to periodicals. McKay’s 1888 and 1889 impressions of Leaves of Grass conclude with “Sands at Seventy,” sixty-five of these periodical poems first gathered in November Boughs, a miscellany of Whitman’s poetry and prose published the same year. The pages were renumbered to fit the larger collection and serve as an “Annex to preceding pages.” Three years later in the Deathbed Edition, “Sands at Seventy” became the “1st Annex” when Whitman incorporated the thirty-one poems from another miscellany, 1891’s Good-Bye My Fancy, as the second annex (the prose from both volumes was rehoused in McKay’s edition of Whitman’s Complete Prose Works, available on the Walt Whitman Archive). Like the books from which their contents derive, the annexes have a miscellaneous quality, though Whitman’s musings on his impending death are prominent throughout. Also from November Boughs came “A Backward Glance o’er Travel’d Roads,” a retrospective in prose that stitches together previously-published essays on the background of Leaves of Grass, and first included in Whitman’s seminal volume in 1889. Thus the Deathbed Edition employs prose to bring to a close Whitman’s poetic project, which of course was launched in 1855 with a prose preface promising readers that “a great poem is no finish to a man or woman but rather a beginning” (Information on the annexed poems and the “Backward Glance” essay can be found in the introductions to November Boughs and Goodbye My Fancy on the Walt Whitman Archive.)

div.head: The 1891-92 Leaves of Grass: Whitman’s Last Christmas Present
div.p: As is the case with Whitman’s other late-life books, Horace Traubel’s With Walt Whitman in Camden documents the day-to-day creative process behind the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass from the perspective of Whitman’s amanuensis. In early August of 1891, Whitman asked Traubel to get a count of the unbound sheets of Complete Poems & Prose and Leaves of Grass left with Frederick Oldach, the Philadelphia bookbinder who had also worked on November Boughs and Good-Bye My Fancy. Traubel dutifully reported that Oldach had 175 unbound copies of Leaves of Grass and 181 copies of Complete Poems and Prose. Whitman revealed his intention to have the sheets made into paperbound editions, even against objections from his publisher, David McKay. McKay’s “publisherial canniness don’t see the whole panorama,” Whitman said, “there are certainly paper editions of the poets—ought to be—and they might be made to pay.” While the lucrative benefits of putting out a cheap edition appealed to the poet, Whitman later noted that “it is my notion something will have to be added” to the 1881 Leaves of Grass, referring to the poems from November Boughs and Good-Bye My Fancy. Trabuel captures the ailing Whitman’s urgent view of the project: “It is a closing act—the last on the bill: soon the curtain will be down.”

Convincing McKay to issue a paperbound edition was a challenging task, but Traubel was firm and recorded “a good deal of fencing” on October 5th with the publisher who was “opposed utterly to [a] cheap edition.” Eventually the meeting settled two important questions: the binding was to be solid green cloth and the price set at two dollars. When his amanuensis reported back, Whitman quickly approved the cover and the price, emphasizing that “our point is of course to add the pages; whether we make any gain beyond that is not so important.” Again he insisted on a “cheap paper edition,” but left it to the future and ended on a reflective note: “I am so happy to have lived out the work, to have touched the last mile-point—actually, I have rounded Leaves of Grass—that I am willing to sacrifice most else.” (Perhaps responding to this sullen tone of self-sacrifice, Traubel continued to press McKay for a paperbound edition which was released in January 1892 and priced at fifty cents—McKay had planned to charge eighty-four cents for it until Whitman insisted the price be lowered.)

By November 1891, Oldach was binding pages of Leaves of Grass with the annexes. Whitman intended to send some copies of this “complete” edition as Christmas presents, but Oldach’s other Christmas orders meant significant delay in finishing Whitman’s books. Toward the end of the month, Whitman directed Traubel to order 100 copies stitched in brown paper covers with yellow labels. “I thought the matter over a good deal and concluded this as good a way as any to settle it,” the poet declared. In a “killing two birds with one stone” arrangement, Whitman could have cheap paperbound copies of Leaves of Grass and they could be done in time for Christmas. About a week later, Oldach sent Whitman a sample of the paper cover which he approved. The first four days of December, Whitman eagerly pressed Traubel for any news of the books, “almost worried to see them,” Trabuel observed.

On December 5, an excited Traubel entered Mickle Street “with a big bundle under my arm” containing ten paperbound books from Oldach, sample copies to ensure that Whitman liked the brown paper covers. “Here is my book at last!” Whitman exclaimed, “Into harbor at the end of day!” He had a list of recipients for the gift copies, including John Johnston and J. W. Wallace in England, and must have sent them out right away, since Bucke wrote on December 8th to thank him for the gift. Whitman wanted a few adjustments to the title page and to consider other covers, and a few days later received some copies bound in grey paper that he preferred to the brown. The green cloth binding would not be ready until after the holidays. “Meantime, these will do us,” Whitman told Traubel as he held up the paperbound edition of his complete Leaves of Grass. “I like this cover—this paper cover.”

As more bound copies of the new edition arrived from the publisher, Whitman confided in Traubel that he was “about finished with all deliberate tasks,” and added that he was “more and more mystified about the future” of Leaves of Grass. In the new year, he told Traubel that “the future of the book will have a curious history, no doubt: you will see it—a part of it—I will be gone—a good deal is still left in your hands to do.” Later, Whitman solemnized Traubel’s role in the future of Leaves of Grass in words that, at least as Traubel recorded them, have an odd mix of formal and informal registers: “I authorize you—give you full authorization—to go on just as if you were Walt Whitman—and of course Dave [McKay] understands the relationship.” McKay did not come to appreciate Traubel’s “authorization,” and had a severe fallout with the literary executors following Whitman’s death.

It is understandable that Whitman felt a sense of urgency to complete Leaves of Grass and to hand its production over to his trusted literary executors, since his health had been in decline for nearly a decade. Thankfully, bodily illness did not correlate with cognitive decline, and the decade from 1881 to 1891 was amazingly productive given Whitman’s condition. When the last of the paperbound copies of Leaves of Grass arrived from Oldach on December 12, Traubel brought them over to Mickle Street and assessed that the poet was “in very happy spirit, full of fire and thought.” The following day, however, he found Whitman “strangely and ominously feeble.” With his work on the book completed, Whitman stopped taking the medicinal and alcoholic stimulants on which he relied during the process, and subsequently felt constantly fatigued.

The next week, a languishing Whitman was coughing up mucous and had serious difficulty breathing. “I expect that within four or five days, or in about that time, this mucus will so thicken as to quietly drown, suffocate him,” Whitman’s Philadelphia doctor, Daniel Longaker, told a concerned Traubel, who notified the press to prepare for Whitman’s death and rallied the literary executors for a final review of Whitman’s will. As Longaker was not licensed in New Jersey, he consulted Dr. Alexander McAlister of Camden who agreed that the poet’s life would be over within the week.

Some have objected to the term “Deathbed Edition” because Whitman did not die while making the final edits to the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass. Of course, we know the end of the story and that Whitman survived into March 1892, but for those around him, it seemed like his end was inevitable in late December 1891. For several nights, reporters patrolled past his Mickle Street home and his executors stayed by his bedside past midnight. The day before Christmas Eve, Traubel relates that Whitman was “looking worse than at any time since he had been sick,” his cheeks sunken and his face a deathly blue. With his right lung collapsed, Whitman slept on his left side with “mouth wide open, as if to get over severe difficulties of breathing—the breath itself seeming thick and portentous.” An urgent telegraph to Ingersoll despaired, “All hope gone. May die today or tomorrow.” Similar telegrams went to the disciples in Bolton, England. On Christmas Eve, Whitman gave John Burroughs two copies of the new paperbound Leaves of Grass, grateful to have them available as parting gifts to his longtime friend and supporter who had rushed to Camden for a final visit.

Bucke initially doubted Whitman would survive Christmas Day, though by the late morning he came to suspect that this downturn might not prove to be fatal, a professional opinion not shared by Longaker and McAlister. When Traubel arrived that morning, he found Whitman’s housekeeper Mary Davis in a surprisingly colorful dress. “Whitman said a funny thing today,” Davis told Traubel; “ He saw me flitting about with my black dress on and said to me, ‘O Mary! I wish you would not wear that dreary dress.’” Traubel does not record if Davis put on the black dress out of habit or in preemptive mourning, but Christmas had a generally mournful mood at the house on Mickle Street, despite Bucke’s opinion that Whitman might still pull through. Whitman received visits from John Burroughs, his brother George, and his niece Jessie. For much of the morning, George and Walt were alone upstairs, the younger brother sitting on a box next to the bed. They shared tears and parting words. Between these visits, Whitman faded in and out of consciousness, offering tearful kisses to Jessie and Traubel.

Traubel illustrates Christmas 1891 as a deathbed scene, complete with mourning dress and final goodbyes. Ultimately, however, Bucke’s opinion proved to be more than just a disciple’s optimism. Two nights later, Whitman stabilized and he lived another three months, long enough to see the cloth binding of the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass. Toward the end of January 1892, Whitman held the green book and told Traubel emphatically, “This ‘92 edition is the one to swear by: to us it must, hereafter, be the only edition.” He had been on his deathbed and survived, and this edition of Leaves of Grass had been there, too.

div.head: The “Deathbed” in Question
div.p: Despite the efforts of Whitman scholars to move away from it, there remains an aura around the term “Deathbed Edition.” Although this printing was not publicized as the Deathbed Edition when it appeared and Whitman did not use the term, those who received a copy immediately made a connection between the book and Whitman’s active dying in December 1891. John Addington Symonds, for example, wrote to Horatio F. Brown in January 1892 that “Walt Whitman, from his death-bed, sends me the final edition of Leaves of Grass” (649). He praises the small, paperbound volume as a “beautiful book,” and adds that “at last his life-work reaches a form in which it will snuggle to a man’s breast and lie there—what he always wanted,” tying the volume to Whitman’s longing in Calamus for a reader who will “[thrust] me beneath your clothing, where I may feel the throbs of your heart.” Symonds also confides in Brown that Whitman is “dying hard” and that the Camden disciples keep him regularly updated on the poet’s condition. “All of him, but his heart, is dead,” Symonds concludes; “He lives and lives and longs for death” (emphasis in original).

A month later, Symonds wrote again to Brown that he gets “a daily letter” from Traubel, Whitman’s “devoted friend there.” Symonds’s responses to Traubel preserved in With Walt Whitman in Camden make frequent reference to Whitman’s “death bed” and “sick bed,” and while Whitman’s other disciples eagerly desired the poet’s recovery—Traubel never refers directly to Whitman’s “deathbed,” even when the poet is finally dying—Symonds confesses to Brown a different hope:
I wonder what the meaning of this clinging on to life is, in persons who surround a death-bed? Is it callousness in myself which makes me rather, in these circumstances, pray for a speedy dispatch, a euthanasia, when the whole sad scene would not have to be overacted again? (662-663, emphasis in original)
Symonds was quite open in his letters about the wish that Whitman have a mercifully quick death. A letter to Edward Carpenter counsels that “we must not call him poor or commiserate him, but would that he could be released” (653). For Symonds, Whitman’s release from pain through death unquestionably was tied to the release of Whitman’s 1891-92 Leaves of Grass.

By the end of February 1892, Symonds was certain that Whitman’s time was near, no doubt indicated by those daily letters from Traubel. In a letter to Traubel scrawled in “the dead hours of the night” on February 28, Symonds lays bare his indebtedness to Whitman in full eulogistic mode. “I pour all this out upon you now, because, while Whitman is lying on his deathbed, you must hear what one of his disciples—a man sworn to him unto the grave—has to say about the effect of his prophecy.” Symonds’s letter includes a dramatic postscript, directing Traubel to be sure to “whisper in his ear that so long as I live I shall endeavor to help on his work, & to the best of my poor ability shall try to do this in his spirit” (668). Traubel included an edited version of the letter in his 1892 eulogic collection, At the Graveside of Walt Whitman, among what he called “Sprigs of Lilac,” a compilation of letters from prominent figures including William Michael Rossetti and Alfred Lord Tennyson. (Symonds joined his poet-prophet in death a little more than a year later, as did Tennyson who died in October 1892.)

While we do not know if biographer and bibliophile Isaac Hull Platt also received a copy of the paperbound Leaves of Grass in December 1891, he similarly connects the book to Whitman’s active dying in his 1904 biography of Whitman. Platt’s fairly comprehensive chronology which includes the poet’s strokes in 1873 and 1888, notes that Leaves of Grass was issued in December 1891 only after “the final proofs being passed by him while on his death-bed” (xx). And the book’s annotated bibliography suggests an even more active involvement in both the standard editions of Leaves of Grass and Complete Prose Works as “revised by him upon his death-bed” (141, emphasis mine). In Platt’s story of Whitman, the scene of the dying poet looking over proofsheets is crucial to understanding the relationship between Whitman and his work (111):
Not the least remarkable feature of Whitman’s career and that of his book is the singular pertinacity with which he carried out the work he had determined upon. It was his original intention that it should cover his whole lifetime, and from this plan he never swerved nor faltered. The book was planned before he was thirty years of age, actually begun a little later, and completed only on his death-bed.
In death, the life story of a self has its inevitable lysis. Death is then indispensable if Leaves of Grass is to actualize Whitman’s proposal that “this is no book, who touches this touches a man”; and while Leaves of Grass features poems explicitly about Whitman’s aging and death, Platt’s depiction of a deathbed editorial scene places the book itself—and the reader—directly into the poet’s intimate experience of dying. Death is not only in its composition and contents but in its very construction.

In 1919, a few years after Platt’s death, his extensive Whitman collection went to auction and included every edition of Leaves of Grass after 1860. While the auction catalogue is fairly comprehensive with detailed descriptions of each book offered for sale, noting for instance, the “suppressed edition” of 1881, it does not refer to the 1891-92 Philadelphia printing of Leaves of Grass as the “deathbed edition,” suggesting that the term was not then in common use. Indeed, while Platt’s biography of Whitman and Symonds’s private letters attest to a correlation between this printing of Leaves of Grass and the scene of Whitman’s active dying in December 1891, no direct reference has been found to a “deathbed edition” of Leaves of Grass prior to 1925.

The New York Public Library had an incomplete collection of Whitman editions when it hosted its first Whitman exhibition, sponsored by the American Authors Club in 1925. The library relied on rare book dealer Alfred F. Goldsmith’s extensive expertise in Whitman’s bibliography and broad connections to collectors of “Whitmania.” By the time the exhibition opened on November 7, Goldsmith had managed to fill around twenty cases with items from seventeen collectors, including longtime friend of the poet Bertha Johnston, the archives of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, and biographer Emory Holloway. Holloway seems to have been especially involved in the process, and wrote the exhibition’s official review in the November 1925 issue of the Bulletin of the New York Public Library. “Never before has such a complete list of Whitman editions been on public display,” Holloway wrote.

Eight display cases were filled with printings of Leaves of Grass, numbering almost one hundred and fifty books arranged chronologically with carefully written bibliographic guides. Visitors could see seven copies of the first edition in its variant bindings and the second edition of Leaves of Grass that Whitman presented to Henry David Thoreau. They could see the Osgood Edition of 1881 “which caused such a furore because of threatened legal prosecution,” and the “Pocketbook Edition” from 1889 “which Whitman himself thought his most handsome one.” It is in Holloway’s review of these catalogued “editions,” printings, and impressions of Leaves of Grass that we find the first known published reference to the “Deathbed Edition,” a “small issue hastily bound for Whitman just before his death in order that he might make a farewell present to his friends.” According to the New York Public Library’s report following the exhibition’s close in January 1926, over fifty-six-thousand people filed past Goldsmith’s curated display of editions (43).

Holloway repeats the epithet “Deathbed Edition” in his 1926 volume, Whitman: An Interpretation in Narrative. But while Holloway’s review of the NYPL exhibition is the earliest found mention of a “Deathbed Edition” in print, he makes no claim to originating the term. That claim would be made by a trusted Whitman associate whose work appears in the exhibition’s display cases dedicated to books written about Whitman: William Sloane Kennedy. The year after the exhibition, tucked into the annotated bibliography of Kennedy’s The Fight of a Book for the World, is his description of that final printing during Whitman’s lifetime (250-251):
This I call the death-bed edition. In his last illness, Walt sent to some of us copies of the Leaves volume of this edition, bound in soft Quaker gray paper with printed yellow label on back. . . .The bulk of the edition bound in green cloth; on back of cover, “Leaves of Grass. Complete 1892, Walt Whitman.” A paper-covered bunch of this edition issued in 1892 by McKay at 50 cents.
Kennedy’s lack of capitalization or quotation marks around “death-bed edition” suggests that he is using the term colloquially rather than as an authoritative title like Holloway does. And while some Whitman scholars follow Holloway’s insistence that “Deathbed Edition” only be applied to those rare paperbound copies that Whitman sent out for Christmas in 1891, Kennedy does not make such a distinction. This entry suggests that for him, even the green cloth issue of this last “authorized” edition during Whitman’s lifetime is the Deathbed Edition.

It is true, then, that Whitman did not coin the term “Deathbed Edition,” but it has the same intimate quality of “Author’s Edition” that he had used for special printings of Leaves of Grass since 1876 or the promise on the title page of the 1888 Complete Poems & Prose that he had personally “handled” every copy. This “edition intimacy,” as it could be called, imbues the physical book object with the intimacy between poet and reader performed throughout the text. The Deathbed epithet’s staying power is attributable to many causes, including to the concurrence in December 1891 of the paperbound editions and the fears that Whitman would not survive Christmas Day, which led to the epithet’s likely coinage by his close disciple William Sloane Kennedy, and its later popularization by the prominent scholar Emory Holloway at the first major celebration of Whitman’s acceptance into America’s literary canon. The first recipients of the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass felt transported to Whitman’s bedside at Mickle Street, a sensation that is still possible for the readers who take the edition on its own terms and are willing to encounter its contents in the jagged and messy order in which the poet left them.
